HEADLINE: Builder faces $13m cladding claim
TEXT:
Builder Hickory Group has put subsidiary H Buildings into voluntary administration just days before the subsidiary was due to face a $13 million tribunal claim to replace the combustible cladding on four residential buildings.

While calling in the administrator halts the claim by the 133 owners of apartments in the development in Melbourne's inner eastern Richmond against the builder, it does not resolve the growing crisis that threatens apartment values around the world and is drawing builders, developers, architects and other consultants into a legal fight about responsibility.

"It was a global blind spot and multiple stakeholders are responsible for it," Hickory managing director Michael Argyrou said on Monday. "It's not going to be sorted out in VCAT."

Fallout from the global blind spot will be large in Australia, as governments such as in NSW are not just prohibiting the use of combustible polyethylene-core aluminium panels on new buildings, but requiring structures built with it - even at a time when it may have complied with regulations - to replace that cladding.

"This is bigger than what most people think," said a lawyer involved in cladding issues.

Combustible cladding forces insurance premiums higher, devalues apartments and even makes apartments unsaleable, as the owners of one apartment tower in Manchester in northern England have found.

Liability around the use of combustible polyethylene-core cladding in residential buildings is complicated. The Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal - the same forum that was due to hear the case against H Buildings - will next week begin a scheduled 30-day claim for damages by the owners corporation of Melbourne's fire-damaged Lacrosse building against builder LU Simon.

In that case - in which the owners are seeking $24 million in recladding costs, lost rent and higher insurance costs in relation to the 2014 fire that raced up 13 storeys of the residential tower in as little as 10 minutes - LU Simon is seeking to sheet blame for the use of non-compliant combustible aluminium panels on to its building surveyor, architect, fire engineer, project manager and even residents of the apartment in which the fire started.

Hickory, a prefabricated building pioneer which developed the Unitised Building modular business in Australia with architect Nonda Katsalidis, put the H Buildings entity into voluntary administration earlier this month. A compulsory conference between the builder and the Stawell Street owners corporation was scheduled in VCAT on Wednesday. In total, H Buildings faces 13 claims, two of which are cladding-related. The rest relate to building defects. The other cladding case was minor compared with the Stawell Street claim, administrator John Lindholm of Ferrier Hodgson said.

He said the objective would be a deed of company arrangement, under which all apartment owners would vote for a resolution, rather than liquidating the company.

Lachlan Ingram, a lawyer representing the Stawell Street owners corporation, said on Monday his clients declined to comment.

HEADLINE: Gentle humour the key to urban tales of playwright Neil Simon
TEXT:
New York | When master playwright Neil Simon accepted the Mark Twain Prize for American Humour in 2006 he was visibly nervous. But his gentle humour was evident.

"It took me six years to write my first play," he said, recalling that he found the title for Come Blow Your Horn from one of his daughter's nursery rhyme books.

He said it turned out to be "a so-so play" that was turned into "a so-so movie" with Frank Sinatra.

But it was successful enough that Simon considered calling his subsequent works The Sheep's in the Meadow and The Cow's in the Corn.

"For the first time," he said, "I had money in the bank. Yes, sir, yes sir, three bags full!"

Simon, who died on Sunday (Monday AEST) at 91, was a meticulous joke-smith, peppering his plays, especially the early ones, with one-liners and humorous situations that critics said sometimes came at the expense of character and believability.

No matter. For much of his career, audiences embraced his work, which often focused on middle-class, urban life, many of the plots drawn from his own personal experience. His characters battled depression, alcoholism and loneliness.

Simon's stage successes included The Odd Couple, Barefoot in the Park, the Brighton Beach trilogy, The Prisoner of Second Avenue, Last of the Red Hot Lovers, The Sunshine Boys, Plaza Suite, Chapter Two, Sweet Charity and Promises, Promises.

Many of his plays were adapted into movies and one, The Odd Couple, even became a popular television series.

For seven months in 1967, he had four productions running at the same time on Broadway: Barefoot in the Park, The Odd Couple, Sweet Charity and The Star-Spangled Girl.

Simon's ability to recognise life's little annoyances - too many pillows piled on a sofa, being told as a kid you may not eat any more cookies - connected with audiences. A scene in The Odd Couple when Felix Unger passive-aggressively leaves a note on Oscar's pillow - "We're all out of Corn Flakes. F.U." - got huge laughs.

Randi Mayem Singer, who co-penned the film Mrs Doubtfire, mourned Simon as a "truly great American storyteller". "If you write comedy, if you write period, you learned something from Neil Simon," Singer said.

Big Bang Theory creator Bill Prady wrote: "There is no American comedy writer whose work isn't influenced by the rhythm and music of Neil Simon's words."

Simon was the recipient of four Tony Awards, the Pulitzer Prize, the Kennedy Centre honours (1995) and, in 1983, he even had a Broadway theatre named after him.

The bespectacled, mild-looking Simon (described in a New York Times magazine profile as looking like an accountant or librarian who dressed "just this side of drab") was a relentless writer - and rewriter.

"I am most alive and most fulfilled sitting alone in a room, hoping that those words forming on the paper in the Smith-Corona will be the first perfect play ever written in a single draft," Simon wrote in the introduction to one of the many anthologies of his plays.

Simon's own life figured most prominently in what became known as his Brighton Beach trilogy - Brighton Beach Memoirs, Biloxi Blues and Broadway Bound - which many consider his finest works.

In them, Simon's alter ego, Eugene Morris Jerome, makes his way from childhood to the US Army to finally, on the verge of adulthood, a budding career as a writer.

Simon originally started as a radio and TV writer with his older brother, Danny. Yet Simon grew dissatisfied with television writing and the network restrictions that accompanied it.

Simon was married five times, twice to the same woman. He is survived by his fourth wife, actress Elaine Joyce; two daughters, Ellen and Nancy; three grandchildren; and one great-grandson.

HEADLINE: China's industrials cut costs
TEXT:
Shanghai | Profit growth at large Chinese industrial companies fell in July, but the debt they carry is at a two-year low as fears grow about the fallout of the US trade war on the country's highly leveraged economy.

Industrial profit growth was 16.2 per cent in the month, compared with 20 per cent in June, according to the Nation Bureau of Statistics (NBS). Industrial profits increased 17.1 per cent for the first seven months of the year, to 3.9 trillion yuan.

Profits at state-owned industrial companies rose 30.5 per cent, according to the data, while profits for foreign industrial companies, which includes businesses from Hong Kong, Taiwan and Macau, only rose 7.5 per cent.

The petroleum industry accounted for a large percentage of the overall increase in profits, at 21 per cent. Ferrous metal makers generated 114 billion yuan, or 20 per cent of the total profit increase for the seven months to the end of July. Construction materials and chemicals also contributed.

China said costs continued to decrease for the first seven months of the year and debt carried by large companies fell.

The debt-to-asset ratio for industrial firms declined 0.5 percentage point to 56.6 per cent. The debt-to-asset ratio of state-owned enterprises was 59.4 per cent, down 1.3 percentage points. China said was the lowest level since 2016.

Didi suspends service after rape, murder

Didi Chuxing, China's popular ride-sharing service, fired two senior executives and suspended a carpooling service after the second killing of a female passenger in three months. The crime follows others that have raised questions about the company's ability to protect women who use its services and comes at a fraught time for Didi, one of the world's most successful start-ups. The passenger, surnamed Zhao, used Hitch, the Didi carpooling service, in the eastern city of Wenzhou on Friday. That afternoon she was raped and stabbed in the neck, Wenzhou police said. The driver was arrested Saturday. The scandal provides more fodder for critics of the company, which bought Uber's business in China two years ago. In May, a 21-year-old flight attendant was found dead after using Didi's Hitch service in the central city of Zhengzhou. Didi said in a statement Sunday that it had fired Huang Jieli, the general manager of Hitch, and Huang Jinhong, vice-president of its customer service operations. NYT

Florida police hunt for shooting motive

Police searched on Monday for a motive in the third mass shooting in Florida in two years, which left two people dead and 11 wounded in Jacksonville, before the gunman killed himself at a video game tournament. Witnesses told local media that the gunman, identified by police as David Katz, 24, of Baltimore, was a disgruntled gamer, angry because he lost Sunday's tournament. It was not clear if he knew his victims. While police have not identified the victims, family members told Jacksonville CBS television station WJAX that the two people killed were Eli Clayton and Taylor Robertson, both of whom were video game contestants. Police said 11 other people were wounded by gunfire and at least two others were injured while fleeing the scene of Sunday's shooting. REUTERS

No role for poll in

Indonesia rate move

Indonesia's central bank, faced with a deepening currency rout, won't let an upcoming presidential election prevent it from raising interest rates if necessary. Bank Indonesia is independent and its future policy action will be determined by economic data, Deputy Governor Dody Budi Waluyo said in Jakarta. The bank has raised interest rates four times since May to help stabilise the rupiah, including a surprise 25 basis-point move at its most recent meeting in August. "It's in Bank Indonesia's calculation. If we see that it is the right time to increase the interest rate, we will do it," he said. BLOOMBERG

Iran sacks finance minister after decline

Iran's parliament has voted to fire the country's finance minister amid an economic freefall fanned by America's withdrawal from the nuclear deal with world powers, dealing another blow to President Hassan Rouhani's embattled administration. It's unlikely that the dismissal of Masoud Karbasian on Sunday will staunch the bleeding with Iran's rial currency falling to new lows against the US dollar as high unemployment and inflation haunt the country. However, it shows Iran's Shiite theocracy's growing recognition of the anger felt across the country. "Over the last year since you became the minister, the dinner table of the people has shrunk to the point of invisibility," conservative lawmaker Hosseinali Hajideligani of Isfahan told Karbasian during the legislative hearing. "The purchasing power of the people has dropped down at least by 50 per cent. You have made the people poorer every day." AP

HEADLINE: BIS chief warns of 'perfect storm'
TEXT:
Washington | One of the world's top central bankers has delivered an impassioned warning against the growing threats posed by protectionism, nationalism and trade wars, saying their real-world consequences could unleash a perfect storm.

In a speech widely regarded as one of the highlights of the weekend's (AEST) Jackson Hole gathering of global central bankers, Bank for International Settlements head Agustin Carstens slammed US President Donald Trump's trade escalation as the kind of behaviour that could unleash pain on the world economy - and not just for the US.

"It's paradoxical that the United States is starting to put obstacles in the road at a time when its economy is firing on all cylinders," he told the 42nd annual gathering in Wyoming, hosted by the Kansas Federal Reserve.

Although most of the discussions and presentations at this year's event, which traditionally marks the end of the northern hemisphere summer "silly season", were seen as largely academic and only tangentially related to monetary policy questions, the BIS head's speech was widely noted and applauded.

US Fed officials were largely silent on the risks posed by US trade policy - under which tariffs were slapped on a further $US16 billion ($18 billion) of Chinese imports last week, prompting a commensurate retaliation from Beijing.

However, Mr Carstens - who heads what is often dubbed the "central bankers' central bank" - was less circumspect, saying: "Recent measures to reverse globalisation and to retreat into protectionism alarm me, as they no doubt alarm many of you.

"After decades of setting rules to liberalise trade, we are seeing moves to rip up that rulebook," he said, pointing to the UK Brexit vote, emerging nationalist movements in Europe and the US trade war.

Such efforts are doomed to fail, he suggested, not least because they seek to turn back the clock and "retreat into a simpler world of local production" - undermining the "market discipline that helped curb inflation".

In a direct shot at Mr Trump - who has increased his attacks on US Fed chairman Jerome Powell's gradual interest rate increases - Mr Carstens said tariffs could push up US prices and force the central bank to respond with even faster rises.

"Such a response would widen the interest rate premium to the rest of the world and could drive the dollar higher," he said.

"This would hit US exporters with a double whammy, and emerging market economies with a triple whammy. For emerging markets, a stronger dollar tightens financial conditions, triggers capital outflows and slows growth."

Arguably, all of those things are already under way - complicating the President's hopes of "winning" the trade war.

Mr Carstens also challenged populist, left-leaning politicians and leaders who believe that the dismantling of globalisation will help reverse inequality.

"While higher trade barriers would shield some domestic industries from import competition, the resulting wage gains would be more than offset by the damaging effects of reduced export opportunities and the increased cost of imported inputs for manufacturing firms," he said.

Another worry, he warns, is that today's world of complex production chains and financial links mean the global economy is heavily reliant on a stable dollar.

A decade on from the global financial crisis, it was dangerous to forget how the collapse in trade finance in late 2008 was a key trigger for the recessions that followed.

"We must recognise the potential for real and financial risks to interact, to intensify and to amplify each other.

"Protectionism could set off a succession of negative consequences.

"If all the elements were to combine, we could face a perfect storm," Mr Carstens said.

HEADLINE: OTHER PASSIONS
TEXT:
You have, ahem, a passion for fashion.

Your first big purchase?

It was in the ’80swhen I bought a Chanel quilted bag. I bought it with themoney from an unexpected bonus and spending it on something tangible felt great. I believe there is such a thing as shopping endorphins.

Why do you love fashion?

It’s an important form of personal expression. And it’s one way I get to express my creativity.

Has fashion been a life-long love affair?

Yes. Do you remember that Jenny Kee koala jumper that Princess Diana wore [in 1982]?

I decided that I just had to have one. I grew up in Hobart and there weren’t a lot of shopping options there back then, so I sent away for the pattern and I knitted it myself.

Recently I was in Paris for the Romance was Born show and Jenny Kee was there and I told her I knitted that jumper. She thought that was hilarious.

You have an Hermès Birkin bag. In fact, you have four. What’s the science in getting Hermès to sell you a Birkin?

It’s persistence and patience. I went to the store and I knew one of the assistants, you develop a bit of a relationship, and I put my name down. There was a bit of a wait. I got a black one to start off with, everyone has to have a black one first. Then I got an orange one, a tan one, and one in fuschia.

What’s the attraction?

It’s practical! Especially if you’re a working woman. It’s big enough to put your flats in there, your documents, your iPad. I do have a bit of a bag collection. I’ve got a Boy Chanel, a 2.55Chanel, a Kelly, a Céline… and I like a shoe. I’ve been more adventurous with shoes lately. I’ve got these great silver ankle boots.

Your grab-and-go favourite?

I never thought I would say this, but a white ankle boot can lift any outfit. You wear it with a cut-off pant, a long pant, a dress. It’s a different look, but it works.

How did your career in the law shape your attitude to clothing? Did it make you more conservative?

When I started out I was much more conservative. In those days women lawyers weren’t allowed to wear pants. So when I became a partner at my old firm in Hobart, I wore culottes. That put them all into a spin, and then the floodgates opened.

It’s just about the one advantage of being a woman in the law, you have other options, and the more senior you become, the more you can push. I’m a conservative dresser, but I try not to be boring. I like to have a bit of an edge.

What do your friends and family make of your love of clothing?

They’re very accepting, they know it’s part of me, although I hope that they appreciate that I’m not all about fashion. I suppose there might be the occasional eye-roll.

There’s probably no one less interested in fashion than my husband.

Does the fact he’s not interested in fashion mean h edoesn’t know what those Birkins cost?

He’s told me that he never wants to know.

Name a fashion trend you’ll never adopt.

I have three – fluoro, toe-rings and tattoos.

“You can never be overdressed.”True or false?

False. What you wear, it’s not just for yourself. It’s a way to show respect for whoever you’re meeting with. Dressing appropriately shows you’ve responded to the situation you’ll be in.

Can you explain Melania Trump’s “I REALLYDON’TCARE,DOU?” jacket?

I simply cannot explain that jacket. It’s either bad advice, or negligence. But it’s proof that clothes are powerful. And that’s part of the reason why the numbers of people who attend fashion shows at museums are so huge. For some people, art can be intimidating. Whereas everyone can relate to fashion. ●

HEADLINE: Sense of forebonding
TEXT:
The Great Believers

Rebecca Makkai

Viking

Warning American writer Rebecca Makkai’s third novel might just break your heart. It is a mesmerising tale about the impact of the AIDS epidemic in the 1980s on a close-knit group of gay men in Chicago, told through the eyes of one of them, Yale Tishman. It will stay with you long after you reluctantly turn the last page.

One of the men, Nico, dies of AIDS and the story of his sister, Fiona, is told in parallel, in 2015. It is about Fiona’s attempt to track down her runaway adult daughter, Claire, in Paris. Scarred from watching people she loves die, Fiona has been unable to sustain a relationship or to mother Claire properly.

The novel opens in 1985 at Nico’s wake.

The men are in the prime of their lives – young, beautiful, smart, with good jobs and active sex lives. Little do they suspect what fate has in store. As Yale says later, “I was living in the golden age and I didn’t know it.”

One of the great strengths of the novel is its sympathetic portrayal of the lead characters, particularly the decent and compassionate Yale. We feel his pain as he watches his friends become ill and experiences anger, fear and guilt. Yale is also central to the subplot, about the donation of valuable art by an elderly widow to the gallery where he works.

In Makkai’s unsparing depiction of the devastating effect of AIDS, healthy young men are reduced to “Auschwitz skeletons”, treated as pariahs and beaten up by police at protest rallies.

Discrimination is rife: AZT, the one drug that might help, is the most expensive drug in history. “You think that isn’t pure hatred?” one character asks.

Yet among the horror there is beauty as well. The Great Believers is also about love and friendship, and how tragedy can bring out the best in people. Innumerable acts of kindness happen as Fiona and the healthy men rally around their sick friends.

The Great Believers covers the big themes: love, sex, jealousy, friendship, compassion, betrayal and guilt. It is pervaded by a deep sense of foreboding as the reader wonders which man will be struck down next. It’s the same sense of impending doom that gay men must have felt at the height of the AIDS crisis.

Notes on a Nervous Planet

Matt Haig

Canongate

Take time to stop and smell the roses. It is a simple message but rarely so well expressed as in British writer Matt Haig’s new non-fiction book, Notes on a Nervous Planet. Haig’s Reasons to Stay Alive about his battle with depression was an international bestseller. Here he writes with insight and clarity about the impact of technology on our mental health and provides practical advice on how to survive in a world where anxiety is at an all-time high.

In a series of short, sharp chapters, Haig diagnoses the modern malaise – overloaded minds, rapidly changing technology, the rise of fake news, a deteriorating environment, an obsession with our appearances, the dangers of the internet and social media.

He then suggests how best to combat the malady, including by changing the way we think. To enjoy life in a world where there is an excess of everything we should “focus on the things we can do, rather than the millions of things we can’t”. And to be happy, we all have to calm down.

A Long Island Story

RickGekoski

Canongate

A Long Island Story is the portrait of a marriage under pressure. Its author Rick Gekoski, an American who has long lived in England, is better known for his non-fiction, but in 2017 he wrote his first novel, Darke, to critical acclaim. This, his second, is based loosely on his childhood.

It opens in 1953, at the height of the McCarthy era. Ben works in Washington DC as a lawyer for the Department of Justice, but his position becomes untenable when his communist sympathies are uncovered. Reluctantly, he moves with his wife Addie and their two children to Long Island, where her parents live. Addie, a social worker, is horrified at the thought of exchanging cosmopolitan DC for the dreary suburbs.

Thus, the stage is set for the gradual unravelling of the marriage, as these “fellow travellers” struggle to reconcile the disappointing reality of their lives with the ideals and expectations of their youth. It may not be the most original of topics, but Gekoski’s take on it is fresh and insightful, and his writing is deft. ●
